newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Former warlord set to become Liberian president.
newsitem.headline: Former warlord set to become Liberian president.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor was set to be formally proclaimed as Liberia's president on Thursday after a seven-year civil war which he was largely responsible for starting.

With three-quarters of the ballots counted from the presidential election, Taylor had an unassailable lead with over 75 percent of the votes and a source close to the Independent Elections Commission told Reuters his final victory margin could be 80 to 85 percent.
The commission said its chairman, Henry Andrews, would announce the final results of Saturday's poll at 11.00 A.M. (1100 GMT).

Taylor's closest rival, Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, a former U.N. executive and the only woman among the 12 candidates, had 9.5 percent of the vote declared so far and none of the others reached five percent.

This prompted Johnson-Sirleaf to declare that Taylor's margin of victory was "statistically impossible." She renewed charges of polling day irregularities, but a close political associate indicated that she would accept the results.

"She is going to make a new statement after the proclamation of the results," the associate told Reuters. "She will offer her party's readiness to participate in Taylor's government, although she herself will not play a role in it."
Two of the other candidates -- Cletus Wortorson and Baccus Mathews -- conceded victory to Taylor in a move that vastly diminished any prospects of post-poll trouble.
Liberia's political leaders have come under foreign pressure to accept the result of the elections which wrap up a regional peace accord on ending the civil war.
"Results of the elections announced so far show that the Liberian people overwhelmingly decided that Taylor should be the president of Liberia," Wortorson told reporters.
"We congratulate Mr Taylor," he added, calling on supporters of his Alliance of Political Parties to back Taylor.
Mathews, a former foreign minister, described the elections as "reasonably free and fair" and called on Taylor's other rivals alleging malpractice to accept the outcome.
"There were problems but they were not massive enough to affect the result," Mathews told Reuters.
Two other former warlords who stood for president -- Alhaji Kromah and George Boley -- criticised the conduct of the elections but did not say what they intended to do.
